newsitem.title: UK: B.A.T shares bounce back, shrug off U.S. news.
newsitem.headline: B.A.T shares bounce back, shrug off U.S. news.

text.p: Shares in British tobacco and insurance group B.A.T Industries Plc bounced back from an early tumble on Friday as analysts played down the impact of a rival's decision to settle U.S. tobacco litigation.
After dropping as low as 460p, the shares were up three pence at 492 by 1434 GMT.
"We saw buyers coming in when the shares came off, a lot of people saw it as a knee-jerk reaction and a buying opportunity," one market-maker said.

Liggett Group became the first tobacco company to admit smoking was addictive and could cause cancer when it settled with 22 U.S. attorneys general on Thursday who had sued to recover health care costs for smokers.

Liggett, the smallest of the U.S. tobacco companies with a two percent market share, has agreed to allow current and former employees -- including its lawyers -- to testify against the rest of the industry.
B.A.T shares plunged six percent in early trade as investors worried Liggett would reveal a "smoking gun" which would prove the states' cases.
But analysts played down the danger.
"This is all hype. I can't believe Liggett has documents which the other tobacco companies don't have," said Tom Bennett, analyst at Banque Paribas.
He said that under U.S. "discovery rules", U.S. tobacco companies have already provided a large quantity of documents to U.S. state legal authorities.

B.A.T said its U.S. division Brown & Williamson had already provided the states with around 12 million pages of documents. "If you lined them up end to end they would stretch from London to Warsaw," B.A.T spokesman Ralph Edmondson said.
"We will not go out seeking a settlement," Edmondson said. "Any move (like Liggett's) will not be initiated by the tobacco companies."
Analysts at Goldman Sachs said B.A.T remained on its global priority list with estimates unchanged, despite the Liggett settlement.
Tobacco shares have recovered in recent months amid indications the U.S. government might be moving towards a settlement of tobacco-related litigation.

B.A.T itself said earlier this month that it would be sensible to evaluate a settlement, which chief executive Martin Broughton said should cover all current and future claims and as approved by Congress and the White House.
